strengths: Addresses genuine gap in generative DyTAG benchmarks; strong problem motivation with clear empirical evidence of limitations in existing datasets (DTGB)
High-quality dataset curation: eight diverse, carefully processed DyTAG datasets with systematic demonstration of superior textual quality compared to existing benchmarks
Well-motivated task formulation: TDGG and IDGG provide meaningful complexity gradient aligned with real-world graph expansion patterns
Comprehensive evaluation framework: multifaceted metrics (structural, textual, embedding-based) more holistic than prior work
Extensive experiments: multiple LLM backbones, comparisons with DGNN and generation baselines, ablation studies, and scalability analysis
Reproducibility support: detailed implementation details, prompt templates, and promised resource release
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: GAG-General is incremental extension of GAG [25]; core contribution is benchmark construction rather than novel generative methods

Textual quality evaluation lacks rigor: LLM-as-Evaluator approach relies on subjective criteria without inter-rater reliability validation or human evaluation; consistently high scores (4.3-4.9) raise concerns about metric discrimination and sensitivity

Questionable evaluation design: Power-law validity thresholds (D_k < 0.15, α ∈ [2,3]) are arbitrary without justification; extended JL-Metric validity not established; no empirical comparison with alternative metrics (BERTScore)

TDGG task formulation concern: With fixed node sets, TDGG is essentially edge prediction/classification rather than true generation; blurs boundaries with discriminative tasks and somewhat misleads regarding generative framing

IDGG complexity inadequately addressed: Limited analysis of why IDGG has higher errors; hub node analysis is anecdotal rather than systematic; unclear whether divergence from ground-truth is beneficial feature or failure mode

Severe scalability limitations: TDGG ~1.6 hours per 10K edges, IDGG ~1.1 hours per 2K edges, large-scale generation 16-35 hours; reliance on expensive LLM APIs prohibits practical deployment and iterative development
Baseline comparison fairness issues: LLM-based generation vs. DGNNs not directly comparable; VRDAG/DG-Gen not designed for text; missing simpler statistical/rule-based baselines
Insufficient error analysis: No systematic failure case analysis, lack of understanding why/when generation succeeds, limited exploration of dataset-specific challenges
Statistical rigor lacking: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; results presented as single means without variance characterization

Reproducibility concerns from LLM dependency: API-based LLM behavior evolves over time; sensitive to prompt engineering and temperature settings; results may not be reproducible with future model versions

strengths: Addresses a real gap: Identifies and validates that existing DyTAG datasets (DTGB) have poor textual quality, with empirical evidence that GDGB improves generation outcomes
Comprehensive dataset curation: Eight carefully selected datasets across diverse domains (e-commerce, social networks, biographies) with rich textual features for both nodes and edges
Well-motivated task formulation: Clear distinction between TDGG (transductive) and IDGG (inductive) generation captures different real-world scenarios
Extensive experimental evaluation: Comprehensive experiments across 8 datasets, 4 LLM backbones, ablation studies, and comparisons with multiple baselines
Multidimensional evaluation framework: Attempts to capture structural, temporal, and textual quality through complementary metrics
weaknesses: Circular evaluation methodology (critical): Using LLMs to evaluate LLM-generated text introduces fundamental bias toward LLM outputs; lacks human evaluation standard for text generation benchmarks, undermining claims of 'rigorous evaluation'

Limited technical novelty: GAG-General is a straightforward extension of GAG [25]; the three enhancements are engineering-level adaptations rather than methodological innovations; no novel algorithms or architectures

Unclear TDGG formulation: TDGG combines traditional discriminative tasks (node retrieval, edge classification) rather than being a distinct generative task; lacks clear problem formulation justifying this as a meaningful generative contribution

Insufficient IDGG analysis: Generated and ground-truth hub nodes diverge significantly (e.g., different product categories); claimed advantages for 'proactive decision-making' are speculative without validation; no analysis of whether generated nodes are realistic vs. random permutations

Unfair experimental comparisons: VRDAG/DG-Gen lack text generation capability making comparisons limited; TDGG baselines are dated (2019-2020); reporting 'best results' across different LLM backbones appears cherry-picked without addressing high variability
Severe scalability limitations: 1.6 hours per TDGG dataset (10K edges), 35+ hours for 50K-100K edges; impractical for real applications with no proposed solutions
Vague graph embedding metric design: Extension of JL-Metric lacks principled justification for concatenating textual features; no handling of variable-length texts explained; missing ablation studies
Inconsistent results across models: Dramatic performance variability across LLM backbones (e.g., Degree MMD 0.110-0.243) raises reproducibility and robustness concerns

Missing critical analyses: No failure case analysis, no human evaluation of text quality, no error analysis identifying which node/edge types are hardest to generate, no qualitative examples with explanations
Power-law validation too coarse: Binary criterion (Dk < 0.15, α ∈ [2,3]) may miss important structural degradation patterns

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in DyTAG research with poor textual quality in existing datasets (DTGB) clearly demonstrated
High-quality benchmark contribution with eight carefully curated datasets spanning diverse domains with significantly enriched textual features
Well-designed task formulations (TDGG and IDGG) that meaningfully capture different aspects of dynamic graph generation and model realistic graph evolution
Comprehensive multifaceted evaluation framework combining structural metrics (MMD, power-law), LLM-based textual quality assessment, and graph embedding metrics
Extensive experimental validation with multiple LLM backbones, ablation studies demonstrating importance of memory components, and comparisons against multiple baselines
Clear presentation and commitment to releasing datasets, code, and leaderboards as a resource for the community
Novel LLM-as-Evaluator approach for textual quality that preserves semantic fidelity better than embedding-based metrics
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: GAG-General is largely an incremental extension of prior GAG work [25] with straightforward generalization to bipartite/non-bipartite graphs achieved mainly through prompt engineering
Significant computational efficiency concerns: TDGG takes ~1.6 hours for 10K edges, IDGG ~35 hours for 50K edges, limiting practical adoption and cost implications of LLM APIs not discussed

Evaluation metric concerns: (1) Textual quality via LLM-as-Evaluator may be subjective without inter-annotator agreement analysis; (2) Graph embedding metric design of concatenating variable-length histories is questionable; (3) Power-law thresholds appear arbitrary without sensitivity analysis
Incomplete baseline comparisons: IDGG compared only against models lacking text generation (VRDAG/DG-Gen) without fair adaptation; TDGG DGNNs trained on only 1,000 edges artificially handicaps them
IDGG hub node divergence (Section 5.3) raises questions about whether models learn distribution properties or just generate plausible text; limited validation that divergent nodes are improvements
Missing error analysis and sensitivity studies: no systematic evaluation of generation failure modes, hyperparameter robustness (random walk length, memory cap), or prompt variation effects
Limited analysis of generated graphs' structural fidelity beyond MMD/power-law metrics; insufficient exploration of what patterns emerge in generation

Dataset documentation gaps: no inter-annotator agreement metrics for curation quality, limited discussion of domain representativeness and potential biases, some datasets relatively small (IMDB: 125K nodes)

strengths: First comprehensive benchmark for generative DyTAG learning, addressing a genuine gap in the field
High-quality datasets with demonstrably superior textual features compared to DTGB across multiple dimensions (length, perplexity, LLM ratings)
Well-motivated task formulations (TDGG and IDGG) that capture realistic graph evolution scenarios
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple LLM backbones, thorough ablations, and multifaceted metrics (structural, textual, embedding-based)
Extensive evaluation on downstream tasks showing generated graphs preserve utility for link prediction and edge classification
Clear presentation and good organization with detailed appendix supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: GAG-General is a relatively straightforward extension of GAG to non-bipartite graphs without significant innovation

Questionable rigor in evaluation metrics: LLM-as-Evaluator uses subjective criteria and suffers from self-evaluation bias (using GPT to evaluate GPT outputs); human evaluation lacks inter-annotator agreement scores
Severe scalability limitations inadequately addressed: TDGG generation takes 1.6 hours for 10K edges, with 100K edges requiring 16+ hours, severely limiting practical applicability
Unresolved semantic drift in IDGG: Figure 12 shows clear performance degradation after 5K edges despite domain constraints, limiting the utility of the approach
Insufficient baseline comparisons: compared methods (VRDAG, DG-Gen) lack text generation support, making comparisons somewhat unfair; missing comparisons with recent LLM-based methods
Limited analysis of results: performance gains in discriminative tasks are often modest; weak connection established between generative quality and discriminative performance
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices (1,000 edge seed graphs, 50 edges per round) with no ablation studies or sensitivity analysis
Missing important ablations on relative importance of evaluation metric categories and analysis of failure modes across dataset types

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear demonstration that existing DTGB datasets lack semantic textual quality (Figure 1), with comprehensive comparison metrics.
Comprehensive benchmark: Eight carefully curated datasets across diverse domains with high-quality textual features for both nodes and edges, addressing a genuine gap.
Multifaceted evaluation metrics: Three complementary metric types (structural, textual, embedding-based) provide holistic assessment beyond prior work.
Extensive experimental validation: Multiple LLM backbones, ablation studies, downstream task evaluation, and supplementary analyses (semantic drift, hub nodes).
Reproducibility commitment: Promised code/dataset release with detailed implementation details and prompt templates in appendix.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: GAG-General is primarily an incremental adaptation of the existing GAG framework (Ji et al., 2025), with the main generalization being support for arbitrary graph topologies—a useful but straightforward extension.

Unclear practical utility: Paper fails to demonstrate compelling real-world scenarios where DyTAG generation is necessary or preferable to discriminative approaches. Downstream improvements are modest (ΔAP: 0.027–0.108).

Weak baseline comparisons: TDGG compared primarily against discriminative DGNNs rather than generative models. IDGG baselines (VRDAG, DG-Gen, TIGGER-I) lack text generation capability, making comparisons unfair.

Mixed experimental results: Only 6/8 datasets satisfy power-law validity in TDGG; only 4/8 in IDGG. Semantic drift analysis (Figure 12) reveals concerning degradation after 5K edges without domain constraints.
Severe scalability limitations: ~1.6 hours for 10K edges (TDGG), 16+ hours for 100K edges. This makes practical deployment infeasible for large-scale graphs.

Evaluation methodology concerns: LLM-as-Evaluator relies on closed-source GPT-4o-Mini with unclear reproducibility. Textual quality scores cluster near 4.x/5, suggesting evaluator bias. Human validation limited to 50 samples.

Artificial task design: TDGG and IDGG distinction is primarily whether node generation is called first—feels like a hyperparameter choice rather than a fundamental difference. TDGG essentially frames existing link prediction as generation.

Insufficient dataset quality validation: Curation process under-documented. Several datasets use crawled Wikipedia text, which may not reflect original distributions. Beyond length/perplexity metrics, no evidence text is suitable for generation tasks.
Scalability and stability: Figure 12 shows semantic drift necessitates adding domain constraints, reducing generality. This undermines claims of a general-purpose generative framework.
Missing practical justification: Applications mentioned (e-commerce, privacy) lack experimental validation. Paper doesn't explain when/why generation is preferable to existing alternatives.

strengths: First comprehensive benchmark for generative DyTAG learning, addressing a clear gap where prior work focused on discriminative tasks
High-quality curated datasets with demonstrated textual quality improvements over DTGB (Figures 1, 5-7), validated through empirical generation experiments
Well-motivated and clearly defined generation tasks (TDGG and IDGG) that reflect realistic graph evolution patterns
Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation framework spanning structural metrics (MMD, power-law analysis), textual quality (LLM-as-Evaluator with 5 criteria), and graph embeddings
Extensive experimental validation across 8 datasets, 4 LLM backbones, with thorough ablations, downstream task evaluation, and human assessment
Strong reproducibility: detailed implementation specs, complete prompt templates, code/dataset availability commitment, and 50+ page appendix
Practical validation through data augmentation experiments (F.12) showing generated graphs improve downstream model performance
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: GAG-General is a straightforward extension of existing GAG framework (Ji et al., 2025); core contribution is benchmarking rather than methodological innovation
Heavy LLM dependency creates sustainability risks: requires expensive APIs (GPT-4o), poor scalability (16+ hours for 100K edges), and reproducibility concerns if LLM behaviors/availability change
Significant semantic drift in IDGG after 5K edges (Figure 12) inadequately addressed; domain constraints help but don't resolve fundamental coherence limitations

IDGG evaluation is weaker than TDGG despite being the most novel contribution: degraded structural quality (0.370 vs 0.023 Degree MMD on Sephora), only 4/8 datasets satisfy power-law validity, node generation quality relies on moderate human scores (3.7-3.9) without inter-rater reliability reporting
LLM-as-Evaluator for textual quality is circular (using LLM to evaluate LLM-generated text) and lacks validation that scores correlate with ground truth or human judgments
Limited baseline comparisons: IDGG baselines (VRDAG, DG-Gen, TIGGER-I) weren't designed for DyTAG generation; missing ablations on memory design (parameters lack justification)
Insufficient error analysis: no systematic investigation of failure modes, what patterns are hardest to generate, or learning curve analysis
Statistical rigor concerns: some results lack significance tests or error bars; no inter-rater agreement metrics for human evaluation; unclear if performance differences are significant
